The Yom Kippur War. A major conflict between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria from October sixth to twenty-fifth, nineteen seventy-three. Egyptian and Syrian forces attacked Israel on the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, aiming to retake territories lost in the nineteen sixty-seven Six-Day War. Though Israel ultimately prevailed militarily through rapid mobilization and counteroffensive, the war shattered Israeli confidence in military invincibility and demonstrated Arab armies' modernization and capability. The conflict became a diplomatic turning point. Egyptian success in crossing the Suez Canal provided political space for eventual Israeli-Egyptian peace negotiations, fundamentally altering Middle Eastern geopolitics.

Anwar Sadat, Egypt's president, sought to recover the Sinai Peninsula lost to Israel in nineteen sixty-seven. Hafez al-Assad, Syria's leader, aimed to retake the Golan Heights. The war began on October sixth, nineteen seventy-three, when Egyptian forces surprised Israel by launching a coordinated attack across the Suez Canal on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year when Israeli society effectively shuts down.

Initial Arab successes shocked Israel, which had believed the Bar-Lev Line, fortifications along the Suez Canal, virtually impregnable and harbored assumptions of Arab military inferiority. Israeli Commander Ariel Sharon executed a daring crossing that encircled Egyptian forces. Combined with air superiority and Soviet military supply limitations, Israel reversed the war's momentum.

The war lasted three weeks. Israel's tactical victory involved retaking most territory and advancing on Arab capitals, but at an unexpectedly high cost—nearly three thousand Israeli dead. Diplomatically, the war proved pivotal. Sadat's military performance, though ultimately unsuccessful, restored Egyptian credibility and allowed him to negotiate from a position of restored honor.

U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger brokered ceasefire agreements and subsequent disengagement accords, launching shuttle diplomacy between Israel and Arab states. The war catalyzed the Israeli-Egyptian Camp David Accords in nineteen seventy-eight and the first Israeli-Arab peace treaty in nineteen seventy-nine, fundamentally altering Cold War Middle Eastern alignments and establishing Israel's status as a confirmed regional power.
